# Joint distributions {#sec-joint-distributions}

{{< include ./_extensions/r-wasm/live/_knitr.qmd >}}

<!-- Short draft adapted from the categorical-count examples in lecture 4
     and the diamond overplotting/2D-histogram examples in lecture 5. -->

:::: {.slide-outcomes}

::: {.callout-note title="Learning outcomes & Chapter summary"}

1. **Visualize** combinations of categorical values using count heatmaps and sized marks.

2. **Distinguish** joint counts, marginal counts, and conditional proportions by identifying what is counted and the denominator.

3. **Use** a two-dimensional histogram to reveal concentrations obscured by overplotting, and **explain** the effect of bin size.

4. **Compare** rectangular bins, hexagonal bins, and two-dimensional density estimates, distinguishing counts from estimated density.

:::

::::

## Why bother?

[Knowing how many films are horror films and how many are rated R
does not tell us how many are **both**.]{.slide-bullet}
For that, we need to retain the correspondence between the genre and rating
recorded for each film.

[A **joint distribution** describes how observations are distributed across
combinations of values of two or more variables.]{.slide-bullet}
We have already explored relationships with scatterplots
and compared distributions across groups.
Here we will focus on [counting combinations]{.slide-bullet}:
first for categorical variables, then for two numerical variables.

## Counting categorical combinations

We will reuse the movie dataset from @sec-binned-distributions.
For this example, we keep films with age ratings G, PG, PG-13, or R;
a total of 789 films.

::: {.panel-tabset group="language"}

### Altair {.slide-skip}

```{python}
#| label: joint-movies-setup-alt
#| message: false
import pandas as pd
import altair as alt

alt.data_transformers.enable('vegafusion');  # Facilitate working with large datasets
movies = pd.read_csv('data/movies.csv').query("`MPAA Rating`.isin(['G', 'PG', 'PG-13', 'R'])")
movies
```

### ggplot {.slide-skip}

```{r}
#| label: joint-movies-setup-gg
#| message: false
library(ggplot2)

movies <- readr::read_csv('data/movies.csv') |>
    dplyr::filter(`MPAA Rating` %in% c('G', 'PG', 'PG-13', 'R'))
movies
```

:::

[To show a joint distribution of counts,
we often map the two categorical variables
to the x and y channels in the chart,
and then visualize the combined counts 
as color and/or size.]{.slide-bullet}
Color and size then provide two cues to the same quantity.

## Counts as color and size {.content-visible when-format="revealjs"}

::: {.panel-tabset group="language"}

### Altair {.slide-skip}

Mapping `count()` to color counts the films for each combination
of the categories on the two axes.

```{python}
#| label: joint-category-circles-alt
#| slide-show: both
alt.Chart(movies).mark_circle().encode(
    x='MPAA Rating',
    y='Major Genre',
    color='count()',
    size='count()'
)
```

### ggplot {.slide-skip}

Computing and mapping  `count()` to color counts the films for each combination
of the categories on the two axes.

```{r}
#| label: joint-category-circles-gg
#| slide-show: both
movies |>
    dplyr::add_count(`Major Genre`, `MPAA Rating`) |>
    ggplot(aes(
        y = `Major Genre`,
        x = `MPAA Rating`,
        size = n, color = n
    )) +
    geom_point()
```

:::

## Ordering categories {.content-visible when-format="revealjs"}

Just like for other charts using counts
we can sort the categoricals according to their count.
This can be particularly effective 
when there are many categories.
[Here we don't sort `MPAA Rating` by count
since that category has a natural order to it
from lowest to highest rating.]{.slide-bullet}

## Ordered count circles {.content-visible when-format="revealjs"}

::: {.panel-tabset group="language"}

### Altair {.slide-skip}

```{python}
#| label: joint-category-circles-sorted-alt
#| slide-show: both
alt.Chart(movies).mark_circle().encode(
    x=alt.X('MPAA Rating'),
    y=alt.Y('Major Genre').sort('color'),
    color='count()',
    size='count()'
)
```



### ggplot {.slide-skip}

```{r}
#| label: joint-category-circles-sorted-gg
#| slide-show: both
movies |>
    dplyr::add_count(`Major Genre`, `MPAA Rating`) |>
    ggplot() +
        aes(
            y = reorder(`Major Genre`, -n),
            x = `MPAA Rating`,
            size = n, color = n
        ) +
        geom_point()
```

:::

## Comparing counts with bars {.content-visible when-format="revealjs"}

Visualizing counts as both size and color
helps make large and small counts visually distinct.
We could also have visualized the counts as a heatmap,
where the size of each mark is a fixed rectangle
and only the color varies by count.
We will see this visualization further down for numerical distributions
as it is more akin to a histogram with the bins more tightly together.
For precise numerical comparisons, position and length are usually easier to judge
than color or area, so a faceted or grouped bar chart can therefore be preferable
(as we learned in @sec-counts-proportions).
One drawback with such a chart
is that it is harder to see patterns in the nested bars
than the systematic 2D grid.

::: {.panel-tabset group="language"}

### Altair {.slide-skip}

```{python}
#| label: joint-category-bars-alt
#| slide-show: both
alt.Chart(movies).mark_bar().encode(
    y=alt.Y('Major Genre').sort('x'),
    yOffset=alt.X('MPAA Rating'),
    color='MPAA Rating',
    x='count()',
)
```

### ggplot {.slide-skip}

```{r}
#| label: joint-category-bars-gg
#| slide-show: both
movies |>
    dplyr::add_count(`Major Genre`) |>
    ggplot(
        aes(
            y = reorder(`Major Genre`, -n),
            fill = `MPAA Rating`,
        )
    ) +
    geom_bar(position = 'dodge')
```

:::

### Counts or proportions?

::: {.callout-default .ex-prompt}

[There are 134 R-rated dramas and 60 R-rated horror films in this dataset.
Does that mean the horror genre is less concentrated in R-rated films?
What additional information do we need?]{.slide-bullet}

:::: {.callout-default .ex-hint}

[The number of films in a genre and the proportion with a particular rating
answer different questions.]{.slide-bullet}

::::: {.callout-default .ex-solution}

[We need the genre totals: there are 275 dramas and 77 horror films.
About 49% of the dramas are rated R, compared with about 78% of the horror films.]{.slide-bullet}
Drama contains more R-rated films in absolute terms,
but Horror has a larger R-rated share.

For example, the same count of 60 R-rated horror films can be divided by:

| Denominator | Question answered | Result |
|:--|:--|--:|
| All 789 included films | What share are both Horror and rated R? | 7.6% |
| All 77 horror films | What share of Horror is rated R? | 77.9% |
| All 262 R-rated films | What share of R-rated films is Horror? | 22.9% |

[Dividing every cell by the grand total gives **joint proportions**.
Dividing within a row or column gives a **conditional distribution**.]{.slide-bullet}
State the denominator when displaying proportions:
the appearance of a heatmap alone does not tell us which question it answers.
:::::
::::
:::

## Overplotting and binning quantitative variables {#binning-quantitative-variables}

For numerical variables, a scatterplot shows the observed value pairs directly.
But with many observations, overlapping marks can make regions with quite different
numbers of observations look similarly crowded.
[Drawing every observation can saturate a scatterplot,
making very different concentrations look equally dense.]{.slide-bullet}

We will use all 53,940 observations from the `carat` and `price` columns of
a diamonds dataset.
Carat measures diamond weight, and price is in US dollars.

::: {.panel-tabset group="language"}

### Altair {.slide-skip}

```{python}
#| label: joint-diamonds-points-alt
#| slide-show: both
#| slide-title: When points overlap
diamonds = pd.read_csv('data/diamonds-carat-price.csv')

alt.Chart(diamonds).mark_point().encode(
    x='carat',
    y='price',
)
```

Smaller, more transparent marks can help reveal some of the overlap.

```{python}
#| label: joint-diamonds-transparency-alt
#| slide-show: both
#| slide-title: Small and transparent points
alt.Chart(diamonds).mark_circle(size=10, opacity=0.3).encode(
    x='carat',
    y='price',
)
```

### ggplot {.slide-skip}

```{r}
#| label: joint-diamonds-points-gg
#| slide-show: both
#| slide-title: When points overlap
#| message: false
diamonds <- readr::read_csv('data/diamonds-carat-price.csv', show_col_types = FALSE)

ggplot(diamonds, aes(x = carat, y = price)) +
    geom_point()
```

Smaller points and a lower `alpha` make the marks less opaque.

```{r}
#| label: joint-diamonds-transparency-gg
#| slide-show: both
#| slide-title: Small and transparent points
ggplot(diamonds, aes(x = carat, y = price)) +
    geom_point(size = 0.6, alpha = 0.3)
```

:::

## From overlapping points to bins {.content-visible when-format="revealjs"}

Since there are so many observations,
the chart becomes "saturated" or "overplotted".
Smaller or more transparent points help,
but eventually even they saturate when there is enough overlap.
To examine where observations are concentrated,
we can extend the histogram idea from @sec-binned-distributions to two dimensions.

[A two-dimensional histogram bins both axes and maps the count in each rectangle
to color.]{.slide-bullet}
Each rectangular cell is the combination of one x interval and one y interval.

::: {.panel-tabset group="language"}

### Altair {.slide-skip}

Bin both position encodings and map `count()` to color.
Here the bin widths are 0.1 carats and 500 dollars.

```{python}
#| label: joint-diamonds-bins-alt
#| slide-show: both
alt.Chart(diamonds).mark_rect().encode(
    x=alt.X('carat').bin(step=0.1),
    y=alt.Y('price').bin(step=500),
    color='count()'
)
```

### ggplot {.slide-skip}

`geom_bin_2d()` computes the two-dimensional bins and fills them by count.
The two entries in `binwidth` set the widths along x and y, respectively.

```{r}
#| label: joint-diamonds-bins-gg
#| slide-show: both
ggplot(diamonds, aes(x = carat, y = price)) +
    geom_bin_2d(binwidth = c(0.1, 500))
```

:::

The broad relationship between weight and price remains visible,
and we can now distinguish concentrations that were difficult to compare
in the crowded scatterplot.
As with one-dimensional histograms, check more than one bin width
when a pattern matters to your interpretation.

::: {.callout-warning}

### Avoid saturated charts

[When a scatterplot becomes so saturated
that we can't be sure how many individual observations there are in a specific area,
we should consider a two-dimensional histogram or density estimate,
depending on the question we want to answer.]{.slide-bullet}

:::

::: {.deep-dive}

## Hexagonal bins

Hexagonal bins are another option for showing joint counts.
Each hexagon has six edge-sharing neighbors, whereas square bins distinguish
edge-sharing and diagonal neighbors.
Hexagons are also more nearly circular.
These properties can be useful, although either bin shape still requires a choice of bin size.

In ggplot, `geom_hex()` computes the counts in hexagonal bins.
It requires the `hexbin` package.
As with `geom_bin_2d()`, `binwidth` controls the resolution along the two axes.

```{r}
#| label: joint-diamonds-hexagons-gg
#| slide-show: both
#| slide-title: Hexagonal bins
ggplot(diamonds, aes(x = carat, y = price)) +
    geom_hex(binwidth = c(0.1, 500))
```

## Two-dimensional density estimates

We can also extend the kernel density estimates from @sec-smoothed-distributions
to two dimensions.
Each observation contributes a two-dimensional kernel rather than a one-dimensional bump.
[The resulting colors represent estimated density,
rather than counts in bins.]{.slide-bullet}
As with a one-dimensional KDE, the smoothing settings affect how much detail is retained.

The following ggplot example displays the estimated density as filled bands.

```{r}
#| label: joint-diamonds-density-filled-gg
#| slide-show: both
#| slide-title: Two-dimensional density
ggplot(diamonds, aes(x = carat, y = price)) +
    geom_density_2d_filled()
```

Contour lines show levels of equal estimated density, rather like elevation contours on a map.
They can be useful, but an unfilled contour plot can be harder to interpret
than a filled density plot.
It does not automatically provide a colorbar, and the outermost contour does not
necessarily cover the full extent of the observations.

```{r}
#| label: joint-diamonds-density-contours-gg
#| slide-show: both
#| slide-title: Density contours
ggplot(diamonds, aes(x = carat, y = price)) +
    geom_density_2d()
```

:::
